parole.testo: From Middle Dutch brasem, from Old Dutch *brasma, from West Germanic *brahsmō, from Proto-Germanic *brahsmǭ, *brahsinō, *brahsmaz (“bream”). Further etymology uncertain; perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrēḱ- (“to shine”) (see English braid (verb)).
From Middle Dutch geluc, further origin unknown. Found only in West Germanic (as a word of native origin). More at German Glück (“joy, bliss, luck”).

Related to Old High German muckezzen (“to pout”), German mucken (“to grumble, be defiant”), Middle Low German mucken (“to grouse, to grumble”), ultimately of West Germanic onomatopoeic origin. Probably not related to Latin mūgiō (“to bellow, moo, bray”).

parole.significato: to be dusky, to be in twilight
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schemeren, from a West Germanic frequentative of Proto-Germanic *skimō (“shadow, spectre”), related to *skīnaną (“to shine”). The -m- probably goes back to an old Proto-Indo-European abstract noun-forming suffix *-mo-, similar to *helmaz.
From Middle Dutch schockelen, found only in West Germanic, possibly ultimately imitative, or otherwise from Proto-West Germanic *skokkōn (“to jolt”). Also compare English shock, French choquer.
